title: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
formal: Do there exist real constants \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every monotone access structure \(\Gamma\) on \([n]\) with \(\varnothing \notin \Gamma\) and \([n]\in \Gamma\), there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with \(\max _{i} \log _{2}|S_{i}|\le K\cdot 2^{cn}\), where \(S_{i}\) is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
why: A worst-case storage benchmark for information-theoretic access control, separating the power of general secret sharing from linear schemes. The newly reported bound directly addresses its strict exponential threshold.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Nir’s August 2026 ECCC report, Theorem 1.5, claims a general scheme with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\), directly implying the stated strict threshold after adjustment of the universal constant. The target and theorem were compared; the proof was not independently verified. This remains an uncertain claimed resolution.

progress.text: Applebaum–Nir give a general upper exponent \(\log _{2}(3/2)\approx 0.585\).
The Dagstuhl seminar poses the strict \(c<1/2\) target; the printed historical exponent differs from the cited construction.
Nir states a matching nonlinear upper bound with exponent 0.496 in Theorem 1.5.

importance.reason: The share size needed for general secret sharing is a fundamental efficiency limit for realizing arbitrary access structures.
importance.basis: Saved question, title, and category scope; importance review only, not a fresh proof or open-status review.

definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). An access structure \(\Gamma \subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is monotone when \(A\in \Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq [n]\) imply \(B\in \Gamma\). A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_{i}\in S_{i}\), where each \(S_{i}\) is a finite nonempty set. For each \(A\in \Gamma\) there is a deterministic map \(r_{A}:\prod _{i\in A}S_{i}\to \{0,1\}\) such that \(r_{A}((X_{i})_{i\in A})=B\) with probability one. For each \(A\notin \Gamma\), the conditional distributions of \((X_{i})_{i\in A}\) given \(B=0\) and \(B=1\) are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding \(\log _{2}|S_{i}|\) up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some universal \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) satisfy the stated worst-share bound for every permitted access structure, or prove the logical negation in Lean. A negative answer must show that for every such \(K,c\) some access structure admits no perfect scheme with that bound, allowing all finite share alphabets and all joint distributions in the definition. The object quantified over is a general scheme; it need not be linear or efficiently constructed.

sentences: Secret sharing lets authorized groups reconstruct a secret while unauthorized groups learn nothing.
The target asks for a universal bound \(K\cdot 2^{cn}\) bits per share for every n-party access structure, with \(c<1/2\) and a one-bit secret.
Perfect reconstruction and privacy are required, and nonlinear schemes are allowed.
Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\) bound that would meet this target.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\). Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and \(1/2\) absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs \(\log _{2} M\), even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is \(1.5^{n+o(n)}\), equivalently \(2^{0.58496\ldots n+o(n)}\). This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy \(c<1/2\).
